subject: forensic-medicine
title: Antemortem Burns, Joule Burns and Electric Marks

steps.title: Proof the victim breathed during the fire
steps.tx: Two findings together are absolute proof of life in a fire: **carbon particles in the terminal bronchioles** on histology and an elevated carbon monoxide saturation in blood. Soot mixed in frothy mucus coats the congested air passages, and incising the trachea before evisceration displays it. Soot merely percolating into the back of an open pharynx after death never passes the vocal cords, so depth of soot is the discriminator.
steps.say: Soot below the vocal cords plus raised carbon monoxide proves breathing during the fire, while throat soot alone proves nothing.

steps.title: Carbon monoxide levels in fire deaths
steps.tx: In fatal burning, blood carbon monoxide commonly exceeds ten percent and may reach seventy to eighty percent, giving the blood its cherry red colour that heat later browns, in **carboxyhaemoglobin interpretation**. Children and the elderly die at thirty to forty percent, and heart or lung disease lowers the fatal level further. Carbon monoxide may be absent after rapid death, flash fire or inhalation of superheated air, so absence alone never proves the body was dead before burning.
steps.say: Fire deaths often carry ten to eighty percent saturation, children die near thirty, and a zero reading still proves nothing alone.

steps.title: Antemortem blisters versus postmortem blisters
steps.tx: Living skin answers heat with inflammation, making **antemortem burn blisters** that carry a hyperaemic red zone around them, a red floor with swollen papillae and fluid containing white and red cells. Postmortem blisters, including those of putrefaction and carbon monoxide poisoning, show no surrounding hyperaemia and no red floor. When considerable destruction has occurred, Reddy warns the two may become genuinely difficult to separate, and the report should say so.
steps.say: A red halo and cellular fluid mark the living blister, while the postmortem blister sits on pale skin with a quiet floor.

steps.title: The electric mark or Joule burn
steps.tx: The **electric mark or Joule burn** is specific and diagnostic of contact with electricity, found at the point where current entered. Heat generated inside the tissues makes round or oval shallow craters one to three centimetres wide, ringed by a ridge of skin one to three millimetres high, with a pale flattened floor. An areola of blanched skin at the periphery survives death and is pathognomonic. Palms are the commonest site.
steps.say: A pale floored crater with a raised rim and blanched halo on the palm is the diagnostic electric entry mark.

steps.tx: Where current enters, heat generated inside the tissues produces the **electric mark or Joule burn**, a finding specific for electrical contact. The lesion is a round or oval shallow crater, one to three centimetres across, edged by a skin ridge one to three millimetres high, and the floor looks pale and flattened. A peripheral areola of blanched skin persists after death and is regarded as pathognomonic. Palms are the usual place these marks are found.

steps.title: When electrocution leaves no mark
steps.tx: Absence of a mark never excludes electrocution under **markless electrocution conditions**. With low voltage and a large wet contact, such as grasping a wire with a wet hand or dying in a bathtub, current spreads and no burn forms. A small contact or a brief touch can also leave nothing before ventricular fibrillation throws the victim off the wire. Moist skin may show no mark while thick dry skin shows a well marked one.
steps.say: Wet wide contact and bathtub deaths conduct without burning, so a clean skin examination cannot clear electrocution.

steps.title: Histology of the electric mark
steps.tx: Microscopy supports the naked eye in the **histology of electrical injury**: the dermis coagulates, the epidermis separates in places, and in other areas cells elongate into parallel rows streaming at an acute angle or almost at right angles to the dermis, as if combed by the current. This streaming of elongated nuclei is characteristic enough that a doubtful crater can be confirmed from a small excised sample sent for sectioning.
steps.say: Combed, elongated nuclei streaming through the epidermis confirm a doubtful crater as a true electric mark.

steps.title: Crocodile skin and flash burns of high voltage
steps.tx: High tension current arcing across the body without firm contact punches out multiple small discrete pitted burns as the arc dances over large areas, the **crocodile flash burns**. High voltage can jump several millimetres at one thousand volts and about thirty five centimetres at one hundred kilovolts. Massive currents char the body, destroy extremities and rupture organs, and bone involvement can elevate periosteum or fracture the bone beneath.
steps.say: Arcing high voltage peppers the skin with pitted crocodile burns and can blast limbs apart without any firm contact.

steps.tx: Without firm contact, high tension current can arc and skip across wide areas of a limb. **Crocodile flash burns** are the many small discrete pits punched out as that arc dances over the skin. At one thousand volts a spark may jump several millimetres, and at one hundred kilovolts the gap can reach about thirty five centimetres. Very large currents char tissue, destroy extremities, rupture organs, and may lift periosteum or break the bone underneath.

steps.title: Spark burns and metal object burns
steps.tx: Where an air gap separates metal from skin, a **spark burn** forms: a central nodule of fused brown or yellow keratin ringed by the typical pale areola, from pinpoint size to deeply contracted with prolonged contact. Metal objects worn or carried, such as rings, buckles and cuff links, fuse in the flash and print true surface burns beneath them. Those same objects, being metal, later help establish identity in burnt bodies.
steps.say: A fused keratin nodule with a pale halo marks the spark gap, and fused jewellery prints burns that later aid identity.

steps.title: Separating burns from scalds and chemical injury
steps.tx: Exam tables love the three way separation of **burns, scalds and corrosive injuries**. Flame burns singe hair, char skin and form thick contracted scars. Scalds leave wet unburnt clothing, no singeing and thinner scars with less contraction. Corrosives add distinctive colour, possible charring and ulceration, with thick contracted scars. Trickle lines of burning kerosene down the neck, trunk and thighs reveal accelerant poured over a lying body.
steps.say: Singed charred skin means flame, wet sodden skin means scald, and coloured ulcerated skin points to a corrosive agent.
